# PART I: The Suit

## 1: Confession
Before I tell you who I really am, allow me to introduce myself.

My name is Edward Claude Hamels. I am, like all of us, many things: The second son of a happy family, a once-promising journalist, a lover of birds,  a decent pianist, and most importantly, a fraud. 

If you are a person who reads _The New York Times_ or is exposed to the bankrupt churn of morning television, you will know me better as the Great Sasquatch of Ticonderoga.

What follows, in the limited time that remains before I am arrested, is a modest account of how I came to be this other creature. I don't know whether that window will allow for a sufficient accounting of that delicate transmogrification, but I will do my best to put down the important points. Bearing in mind that the fine lawmen of Essex County, N.Y. may encounter some difficulty locating a summer cottage that remains a mystery to the United States Postal Service. Anything left unsaid I will do my best to fill in on my forthcoming appearance on Good Morning America.

That is, allowing that the good people of ABC News are able to arrange a recorded interview from inside the Essex County jail.

## 2: Kathleen O'Grady
My name is Edward Claude Hamels. After I graduated college, I flitted about between a variety of small-to-medium publications in Washington, D.C., first as a cub reporter and then, by raw instinct of survival, as a hybrid writer-cum-statistician in what was then the burgeoning niche industry of "data journalism." The first job that I held down for longer than a year, for a criminal pittance, was at _Chalk_ Magazine, an early progenitor of online-only news that specialized in irreverence, to a fault.

That was February of 2006, when the South Wind of the economy was just beginning to gather its velocity and before all but the gloomiest of observers foresaw the coming blackness. It was also a small, forgotten window of time between the end of Geroge W. Bush's hegemony and the formal apotheosis of Barack H. Obama, who would announce his candidacy for president almost exactly one year later. Seeing the writing on the wall, the Republicans unlocked the dog-flap to allow in a class of third-rate candidates who were destined to lose, which is how I came to be aware of<!-- page:0002:01 --> a woman named Kathleen O'Grady, the wife of an early telecom billionaire who enjoyed a small, devoted following of her series of "Our Journey” books that were an incomprehensible mishmash of garden-variety Buddhism, The Secret, generic self-help, and a peppering of sexual memoir that dipped just a toe over the milquetoast diet of American amory. 

Kathleen O'Grady was waging an unwinnable challenge to the superannuated Senior Senator of Maryland, and might have gone largely unnoticed--or at least unacknowledged--by the national media if not for the intervention of an enterprising gossip columnist for one of the Capitol Hill broadsheets, who unearthed a YouTube video of Ms. O'Grady's appearance on the Cindy Candace Show, a daytime gabfest that was typically only on in waiting rooms and workplace gyms. She was there to hawk her third book, "Home and Back Again: How I Rediscovered the Wonders of the Everyday." Cindy Candace asked O'Grady what the most amazing, unexpected thing she had ever witnessed during her month-long sojourn to the Pacific Northwest. I've seen this clip so many times I've committed her response to memory involuntarily: 

“Well, as you know, there is just the most amazing Native-American culture there, particularly in Canada. As I write in the book, I became very close with a young man named Payuk, a fisherman on tha Vancouver Island from the Salishan Tribe who had just the most wonderful stories passed down through the generations. It's what we White People call “mythology," but here's the thing, Cindy: To them, these incredible people, it's real. It's part of the world. So one evening, Payuk and I were walking along the outskirts of a forest when he grabbed my arm and just froze, putting a finger to his lips. It was a clear night, but not much of a moon, and at first I didn't see anything unusual.

“Then, about fifty yards away, in the forest, this tremendous shadow bolts through the trees and just vanishes. We must have waited half an hour without moving, but whatever it was, it never came back. And you know, Cindy, I think that was the first time I really felt a one of those wonderful moments of awakening, as I describe in the book. That there was far more mystery in the world than most of us will ever know.”

I'll say this much for Cindy Candace: She was no slouch. She saw the moment and seized it by the horns. <!-- page:0003:01 -->From here on out, the transcript tells it all.

## 3: POLITICS AS USUAL

August in Washington is normally the time when politicians drop news that
they hope no one will notice, seeing as all of Congress and half the media
have fled the mosquitos for softer climes. Those of us too junior to
afford two weeks in Martha's Vineyard were left to pick up the scraps
of what little news we could be trusted e not to mangle. The column
about Kathleen O'Grady's 2003 appearance on the Cindy Candace show went
online the morning of Tuesday, August 3. By the time I saw it, at around
11 a.m., the YouTube clip had about 6,000 views. By that afternoon, it
had half a million.
At the time, Chalk had a semi-dormant politics blog called "Back of the
Bus" that was hurting for content. The chief contributor, my friend
.wbex, had written a 250-word blurb on the video that morning, and having

BIBLIOGRAPHY, PART ONE

Kathleen O'Grady held out for five days, buttressed, I imagine, but by a
groundswell of encouragements from climate change denialists and vaccine
holdouts that quickly dwindled. The Republican Party wanted nothing to do
with her. On top of George Allen's gibberish fiasco, they were pulling the
chord on anyone and anything who could sully the party's image in the few
races that were still competative. It didn't matter. In November, Democrats
retook he both chambers of Congress and everyone's attention pivoted
overnight to the 2008 presidential primaries.
There was one silver lining, for me. My forays into the shallow end of
computer science had caught the attention of *Chalk*'s editor emeritus,
who was still around in some invented role at the top of the masthead, and
when it came time to either hire me or let me go, he intervened ander the
logic that, for a magazine that existed only digitally, it was useful to
have someone around who knew something about computers. I was hired for
the same salary I had been paid as a contracter, but without the punishing
end of payroll taxes that I was made aware of the following April. I remained
the lowest ranking member of the staff for two years.
I want to say something about computer science here, because I fear the
mere mention of the phrase will send readers running for the fallow earth
of Salinger, or Vonnegut, or Ishiguro, or any other author who bunkered
down, deliberately or otherwise, the the analog. Writing code is its own
variety of poetry frozen in the First Days of the sonnet, when the tyranny
of rhyme schemes and iambic pentameter kept even the wildest bards well
hemmed in. It is equally as lucious and unbounded, at the same time, as
the most modern forms, only it expresses its ideas a shade more deliberately.
More importantly, what I learned of the stronger tongue was critical to
the execution of my second act as a Sasquatch, which was infinitely more
fantastic than the first. Still, I do not intend to dip a single toe into

About Emma: We didn't communicate that following Sunday, and on Monday she
said hello when I got in as though it were any other day. She left *Chalk
about a year later to double her salary at an advertising firm, and gor
some time we lost touch. But we have not seen the last of her.
I happily plied my new trade vocation through the end of 2008, as the economy
went to tatters and Barack Obama won the presidency. If anything stands out
in that interval, it is the distinction that, by one minute, I was the first
journalist to declare Obama the victor on November 6, the moment he clinched
Ohio. My beloved Philadelphia Phillies had won the world series six days
earlier. That was a good week.
There weren't many good weeks after that. One by one, the vanguard of
Washington journalism underwent punishing rounds of layoffs while a breed
of digital suckerfish chewed up the detritus, cornering the market on
available eyeballs through a combination of d@ relentless young reporters
unbounded by the old rules, a glut of unpaid contributors, and dark magic
that floated their single-sourced content to the top of the search pages.
For all its bone fides as the first magazine to forgoe prints, _Chalk_ had
never put much effort into considering what the browser had to offer that
paper and ink didn't. This was the principle reason for my employment, but
I was both unqualified and uninterested in plumbing the depths of the source
code for anything that would make our articles more palatable and available
to the two most important constituencies: Casual readers and the unknowable
algorithms that served up content for them to read. If I had to guess, I'd
say this was a time when the latter's influence outweighted the former and
wrought incredible damage on the dwindling population of reporters who
still worshipped at the shrine of honesty.
I'll say this much about Chalk
_, and Gatz: We did our best to race to
catch up. I was given stewardship of a small team of part-time teenagers
who job was to rewrite stories from the Times and the Post and the news
weeklies in under 250 words. The venerable reporters and columnists, like
Gil Halverson, were perpetually hassled to file three or four times a week
on top of their usual scintillating essays that came in only when they came
in. The advertising outshouted the words on most pages. But we hung on.

BIBLIOGRAPHY
That last chapter referenced Frankenstein in the billing without ever
getting to the point. I certainly didn't make the connection at the time,
but a few days later I did jot down this little passage from one of the
final chapters still several layers down in that delectible onion of a
book:
He ((the monster)) had escaped me, and I must
commence a destructive and almost endless
journey across the mountainous ices of the ocean,
admidst cold that few of the inhabitants could long
endure and which I, the native of a genial and sunny
climate, could not hope to survive. Yet at the idea
that the fiend should live and be triumphant, my
rage and vengeance returned, and like a mighty tide,
overwhelmed every other feeling.
(Shelley, Mary W. Frankenstein. Signet Classic, 1983. pp. 196-19
I hope I needn't belabor the lovely little syllogism here, except to
specify that I am the doctor here and Robbie is the fiend, imitating
the very life I might have given him by accident twice over.
There is another mythology that is more directly relevant here, actually.
This is a local one that comes by way of The Infinite Summer of Roger Finch
(ibid), the book set a mile from Butler's Retreat. l've asked around and
it's genuine, but I'll give James Hallady the mic for a moment to tell it
his way. The story is about Robert Rogers, the eighteenth century militia
leader for whom the mountain kere ew just south of here is named:
Having led most of his 180-man regiment to their deaths,
Rogers found himself cornered at the peak of the mountain
that now bears his name. Before making a run for it, the
story went, he reversed his snowshoes and retreated from
the peak just ahead of his pursuers, so that his tracks
left behind the impression he had gone over the edge.
Clever! Surely apocrphgl, but I wonder now what might have happened if,
somewhere midway along my stroll across the frozen lake, I had contrived
to puncture a vaguely Sasquatch-shaped hole. I can't imagine how this
would have been possible, even if I had been at all equipped for such
hijinks, but I do wonder now if the conclusion would have been that
whatever had roamed the woods of Ti in that winter of 2010 had vanished
forever beneath the surface. (Let's put aside for a moment the fact that
prints of a size 12.5 New Balances led directly to the scene of his

only would have embolded the very realness of the appearances. Would I
now be happily enjoying my freedom, here or somewhere else? Would it have
been enough for Ticonderoga? Enough for me?
No, I don't think it would have been enough for anyone.

93. Room 11

"You wanna call me tomorrow?" she asked by way of farewell.

for that might be. "Get some rest, Ed." And then she was gone.

That was Tuesday, Nov. 2, and it wasn't until an hour past New York City
